synonyms: ["Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome", "Late-stage HIV Infection", "HIV Or AIDS"]
conventional_description: AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, characterized by a severely damaged immune system. It is diagnosed when the CD4 cell count falls below 200 cells per cubic millimeter of blood, or when certain opportunistic infections or cancers develop. Symptoms vary widely but often include rapid weight loss, recurring fever, extreme fatigue, prolonged swelling of lymph glands, and infections like pneumonia or tuberculosis. Without treatment, the body becomes unable to fight off even mild pathogens.
conventional_treatments: The cornerstone of modern AIDS treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART), a combination of medicines that suppress the virus, restore immune function, and prevent progression. Patients also receive prophylaxis against common opportunistic infections and treatment for any active infections or cancers. With consistent ART, many people with HIV never develop AIDS, and those who have can often rebuild their CD4 counts and lead long, healthy lives.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, AIDS is understood as a progressive and profound depletion of the body's vital Qi, with the Spleen and Stomach at the center of the collapse. The Spleen is the engine that transforms food into Qi and Blood - the very substances that fuel immunity. When this engine fails, every organ and tissue is starved of nourishment. This explains why extreme fatigue, poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools are among the earliest and most persistent symptoms.
As the Spleen's weakness deepens, it can no longer produce enough Blood, leading to Qi and Blood Deficiency. The body becomes pale, the mind foggy, and dizziness or heart palpitations may appear. Simultaneously, the body's cooling, moistening Yin fluids can become depleted - a pattern called Qi and Yin Deficiency - because Qi is needed to generate Yin. This dual deficiency brings night sweats, a dry mouth, and a low-grade internal heat that feels like burning in the palms and soles.
These deficiency states leave the body vulnerable to external pathogens. When a surge of Toxic-Heat invades - during an acute opportunistic infection - the weakened defenses cannot contain it. High fever, painful mouth sores, and skin eruptions signal that the body is being overwhelmed. This pattern, while less common, is a medical emergency that requires clearing Heat and toxins immediately, even as the underlying deficiency is addressed.
What makes TCM's view so different is that it does not see AIDS as a single virus attacking a static immune system. It sees a dynamic process of depletion that moves through stages, each with its own distinct pattern. By identifying whether the dominant imbalance is Spleen Qi Deficiency, Qi and Yin Deficiency, Qi and Blood Deficiency, or Toxic-Heat, a TCM practitioner can tailor treatment to exactly what the body needs at that moment - strengthening what is weak, clearing what is toxic, and aiming to restore a functional equilibrium even in the presence of chronic illness.
classical_translation: "When the vital Qi is strong inside, pathogens cannot invade."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about energy and digestion. Profound fatigue with poor appetite, bloating after meals, and loose stools suggests Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency, the most common early pattern in HIV. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels weak, especially at the right middle position.
When night sweats, a dry mouth, and a persistent low-grade fever or heat in the palms and soles dominate, the focus shifts to Qi and Yin Deficiency. This pattern often appears as the illness progresses. The tongue looks red with little coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid, reflecting a loss of the body’s cooling, moistening reserves.
A washed-out complexion, dizziness, heart palpitations, and tingling limbs point toward Qi and Blood Deficiency. The Spleen can no longer produce enough Blood, so these symptoms are more about nourishment than infection. The tongue is pale, and the pulse is thin and weak. This pattern often overlaps with earlier digestive weakness.
During an acute flare or opportunistic infection, high fever, painful mouth sores, and skin eruptions signal a surge of Toxic-Heat. The tongue turns red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and forceful. This excess pattern can erupt on top of long-standing deficiency and requires immediate attention to clear the toxins.

patterns.symptoms: ["Poor appetite and early fullness", "Abdominal bloating that worsens after eating", "Loose or unformed stools", "Profound fatigue and weak, heavy limbs", "Sallow, pale complexion", "Shortness of breath and reluctance to speak"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, Cold, raw, or greasy foods and drinks, Stress, worry, or anxiety, Overexertion, heavy exercise, or physical fatigue
patterns.better_with: Warm, easily digestible, cooked foods, Small frequent meals, Rest and gentle movement, Warmth on the abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Stomach are the body's engine for turning food into Qi and Blood. When HIV depletes the body's foundational Qi, this engine sputters. Food isn't properly transformed, leading to bloating after meals, poor appetite, and loose stools. Without enough Qi, profound fatigue, weakness, and a sallow complexion set in.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy body with tooth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: weak and soft, especially empty at the right Guan (Spleen/Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and simple, cooked foods, which are easier to transform into Qi. Cold and raw foods, as well as overeating, force the already weakened Spleen to work harder, worsening bloating and fatigue. Rest conserves Qi, while gentle movement prevents stagnation without further depletion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals like soups and congees. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods. Eat smaller, more frequent meals to avoid overwhelming digestion. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps Qi flow without depleting it.

patterns.symptoms: ["Night sweats", "Dry mouth and throat with little desire to drink", "Warm sensation in palms, soles, and chest", "Fatigue worsened by exertion", "Shortness of breath", "Low-grade fever"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion, heavy exercise, or physical fatigue, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Hot weather, saunas, or stuffy rooms, Stress, worry, or anxiety, Late nights and lack of sleep, Alcohol and coffee
patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Cool, quiet environment, Warm, moistening foods (congee, soups), Gentle movement (tai chi, walking, qigong)
patterns.why_this_happens: In AIDS, the initial Spleen and Stomach Qi deficiency gradually fails to generate Yin fluids, leading to a dual deficiency. The body's vital energy (Qi) is insufficient to power functions, causing fatigue and breathlessness, while the lack of Yin fluids results in internal dryness and heat, manifesting as night sweats, dry mouth, and low-grade fever.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red or pale-red body with a thin or absent coating, possibly cracked and dry. Pulse: fine (thin) and weak, often rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern stems from insufficient Qi and Yin. Rest and gentle movement conserve Qi, while cool, moistening foods replenish Yin fluids. Overexertion and late nights deplete Qi and Yin further; spicy, drying foods and alcohol consume Yin and generate heat, aggravating dryness and night sweats. Heat exposure and stress stir up empty heat, worsening the warm sensations and low-grade fever.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, moistening foods like congee with goji berries, steamed pears, and black sesame. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods that consume Yin. Prioritize rest and avoid overexertion; gentle practices like tai chi or qigong can help conserve Qi without overheating.

patterns.better_with: Rest and adequate sleep, Warm, easily digestible, cooked foods, Gentle movement (tai chi, walking, qigong)
patterns.why_this_happens: In AIDS, the body's vital energy is deeply depleted, and the Spleen - the organ that transforms food into Qi and Blood - becomes too weak to do its job. Without enough Qi to power the body and without enough Blood to nourish tissues, every organ and limb is starved of what it needs to function. This is why profound fatigue, pale skin, dizziness, and heart palpitations come to dominate the picture.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale body, may be thin or have teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: Fine (thin) and weak, especially in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Rest conserves Qi and Blood, while warm, cooked meals are easy on the Spleen, the organ that produces Blood. Overwork directly burns through Qi, and cold raw foods damage Spleen Yang, impairing digestion and Blood creation. Gentle movement builds Qi without draining it, unlike strenuous exercise which can further deplete resources.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congees, soups, and stews. Include blood-nourishing foods such as red dates, goji berries, dark leafy greens, and small amounts of red meat if tolerated. Avoid raw, cold, or greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking or qigong builds Qi without depleting it. Prioritize rest and sleep to allow the body to repair.

patterns.why_this_happens: In AIDS, the body's vital Qi is already severely depleted. When a surge of external pathogenic toxins invades-during acute HIV infection or an opportunistic infection-the weakened defenses cannot contain it, and the toxins rapidly transform into intense Heat. This Heat flares upward and outward, causing high fever, a raw swollen throat, painful mouth ulcers, and red, pus-filled skin eruptions. At the same time, the Heat consumes body fluids, leading to extreme thirst, dark scanty urine, and constipation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly raised papillae (thorns), dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò) and forceful, often full (实 shí) or overflowing (洪 hóng).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic Heat is an intense internal fire that must be cooled and drained. Cooling foods and drinks directly counter the heat, while rest prevents further Qi consumption. Spicy and fried foods add more heat, and physical or emotional stress stirs up internal fire, making symptoms worse. A calm, cool environment helps the body settle the pathogenic toxins.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: During an acute toxic-heat episode, focus on cooling, light foods like mung bean soup, cucumber, watermelon, and plenty of fluids. Avoid spicy, greasy, or fried foods that add heat. Rest completely in a cool, well-ventilated room; overexertion can worsen the fever and deplete Qi further.

In modern practice, it is also widely used as supportive treatment for heart conditions including heart failure and irregular heartbeat.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure AIDS?
faqs.answer: No, TCM cannot cure AIDS or eliminate HIV from the body. However, it can play a valuable supportive role. Many patients find that TCM helps restore energy, improve appetite and digestion, reduce night sweats, and strengthen the body's ability to cope with infections. It is used alongside conventional antiretroviral therapy, not as a replacement.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs with my HIV medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but it must be done under professional guidance. Some herbs can affect liver enzymes that metabolize antiretroviral drugs, potentially altering their levels. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your HIV doctor about everything you are taking. Never stop or adjust your ART without medical supervision. A qualified TCM practitioner will select herbs that are compatible with your medication regimen.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture help with the fatigue from HIV/AIDS?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is often effective for the profound fatigue that persists even when viral load is controlled. By stimulating points like Zusanli ST-36 and Sanyinjiao SP-6, acupuncture can boost the Spleen's ability to generate Qi and Blood, leading to improved energy levels. Many patients report feeling more alert and less drained after a course of weekly treatments.

faqs.question: How does TCM treat night sweats associated with AIDS?
faqs.answer: Night sweats in TCM are usually a sign of Yin Deficiency with internal heat. The body's cooling, moistening reserves are depleted, so heat rises at night. Herbal formulas like Sheng Mai San, which nourish Qi and Yin, are commonly used. Acupuncture points such as Taixi KI-3 and Sanyinjiao SP-6 help anchor Yin and clear deficient heat. Patients often notice a reduction in night sweats within 6-8 weeks.

faqs.question: What diet should I follow to support my Spleen Qi?
faqs.answer: The most important dietary principle is to eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods that do not tax the Spleen. Think congee, soups, steamed vegetables, and small frequent meals. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, or spicy foods, as well as dairy and excessive sugar, which create Dampness and further weaken digestion. Drinking warm water or ginger tea throughout the day also helps.

faqs.question: Can TCM help prevent opportunistic infections?
faqs.answer: While TCM cannot replace prophylactic antibiotics, strengthening the body's Zheng Qi (vital energy) through herbs and acupuncture can improve overall resilience. When the Spleen and Lungs are strong, the body's defensive Wei Qi is more robust, making it harder for pathogens to take hold. However, always follow your doctor's recommendations for infection prevention and seek urgent care if you develop a fever or signs of infection.

research.title: Analysis of TCM clinical symptoms and signs distribution in 1266 HIV/AIDS patients
research.description: This cross-sectional study analyzed the TCM symptom patterns in 1266 HIV/AIDS patients, identifying the most common patterns as Spleen Qi Deficiency, Qi and Yin Deficiency, and Qi and Blood Deficiency. The findings support the TCM understanding that AIDS is fundamentally a disease of progressive vital Qi depletion with secondary pathogenic invasion.
research.periodical: Author(s) not specified. Analysis of TCM clinical symptoms and signs distribution in 1266 HIV/AIDS patients. Journal of Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine. 2013.

research.title: Retrospect and Prospect of TCM Treatment for AIDS over 30 Years
research.description: This comprehensive review summarized the evolution of TCM treatment strategies for AIDS, including pattern differentiation, commonly used herbal formulas, and acupuncture protocols. It concluded that TCM can improve immune function, alleviate symptoms, and enhance quality of life when used alongside conventional antiretroviral therapy.
research.periodical: Author(s) not specified. Retrospect and Prospect of TCM Treatment for AIDS over 30 Years. Presented at a national TCM conference. 2019.

research.title: Pattern Differentiation and Treatment of AIDS
research.description: This paper discussed the TCM pattern differentiation for AIDS, proposing that the disease progresses from Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency through Qi and Yin Deficiency to Qi and Blood Deficiency, with episodes of Toxic-Heat during acute infections. It outlined corresponding herbal formulas such as Si Jun Zi Tang, Sheng Mai San, and Ba Zhen Tang.
research.periodical: Author(s) not specified. Pattern Differentiation and Treatment of AIDS. Engineering Sciences. Year not specified.
